articles.title_orig: China steps up monetary policy support to bolster stock market
articles.title_zh: China steps up monetary policy support to bolster stock market
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China will step up the use of monetary policy tools to support its capital market, strengthen market resilience and boost investor confidence, its central bank announced Monday.
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) said that it will conduct the third operation of the Securities, Funds and Insurance companies Swap Facility (SFISF) on Tuesday, aiming to help financial institutions secure funding and boost their capacity to buy stocks.
The operation will have a swap term of one year, with the possibility of extension depending on circumstances, according to the PBOC.
A total of 31 securities and fund companies have submitted applications for the facility, with the amount requested exceeding 100 billion yuan (about $14.89 billion), the announcement said.
Introduced in October 2024, the SFISF allows eligible securities, fund and insurance companies to use assets, including bonds, stock exchange-traded funds and shares in companies on the CSI 300 Index, as collateral in exchange for highly liquid assets, such as treasury bonds and central bank bills. The facility is designed to improve participating institutions' access to funding and enhance their capacity to increase stock holdings.
ALSO READ: Fed inaction broadens China options
Industry insiders believe the steady implementation of the swap facility will help put existing assets to better use, facilitate liquidity management across markets such as stocks and bonds, and provide a sustained flow of fresh liquidity to the capital market, thereby encouraging longer-term investment and strengthening the market's inherent stability.
In a statement released Monday, the PBOC said it had held a meeting with the National Financial Regulatory Administration and the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), calling for more effective use of the SFISF and the relending facility for share buybacks and shareholding increases.
The PBOC said it will conduct SFISF operations in a timely manner, expand the number of participating institutions, appropriately lower swap fees, and optimize the collateral and operational arrangements.
"We will work with the PBOC to guide relevant market participants in making full use of the two policy tools and coordinate efforts to support market stability," an official with the CSRC said in response to a media query.
READ MORE: China upgrades e-CNY infrastructure for digital deposit era
The relending facility, launched in 2024 as a temporary measure, will become a long-term arrangement. Its relending rate will be cut from 1.25 percent to 1 percent. Financial institutions are to follow market-based pricing principles, set lending rates reasonably based on the relending rate, and expand lending under the facility.
The central bank conducted the previous two SFISF operations in October 2024 and January 2025, with a combined volume of 105 billion yuan, official data showed.
Meanwhile, loans for share buybacks and shareholding increases have reached about 440 billion yuan in signed agreements, with more than 280 billion yuan already disbursed, helping listed companies finance their market capitalization management activities.
The three departments will step up policy support to stabilize the capital market, strengthen its resilience and boost market confidence, while refining policy arrangements and implementation rules and encouraging financial institutions to make full use of the tools, according to the PBOC statement.
READ MORE: RMB going global serves real economy
The CSRC official said the commission would expand the scope of the relending facility for share buybacks and shareholding increases by listed companies.
The CSRC will urge listed firms that have disclosed repurchase and share increase plans to accelerate implementation progress, and those that have applied for loans to intensify their repurchase efforts, thus sustaining the current sound momentum of stock repurchases and contributing to the stability of the capital market, it said.
"Stock repurchases are an important tool for listed companies to manage their market value, and a key means to stabilize stock prices and convey development prospects and confidence," the official said.
In the first 10 months of this year, 645 listed companies on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges disclosed 700 share repurchase plans totaling 237.7 billion yuan, with the amounts of planned repurchases and actual repurchases both hitting record highs, according to the CSRC.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices are set to be highest for any Election Day in U.S. history
articles.title_zh: Gas prices are set to be highest for any Election Day in U.S. history
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude , the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel.
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.
Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

China’s ruling Communist Party has pledged to target “old nice persons” within its ranks as it steps up its anti-corruption drive ahead of a major leadership reshuffle next year.

articles.content_orig:

Iran said Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States, shortening a process originally expected to take seven days.
The U.N. migration agency said more than 300,000 people in Yemen had fled renewed fighting. China , meanwhile, is sending a special envoy to Iran, Saudi Arabia and Oman .
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Iran's 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, resume nuclear talks
Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.
More than 300,000 Yemenis have fled fighting, UN says
The U.N. migration agency said the people are struggling to find shelter and life essentials, as aid groups face limited access to those in need.
They have fled as renewed fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces broke a four-year truce, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in one of the Middle East's poorest countries.
Taiz province, in southwestern Yemen, continues to take in displaced families, but many are fleeing south to Aden, which has now received more than 56,000 people, according to the latest figures by the International Organization for Migration.
“After years of conflict, families in Yemen are being forced to flee yet again, often with little more than the clothes on their backs,” Abdusattor Esoev, head of the IOM's mission in Yemen, said Sunday.
“They urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care. Without more funding, thousands of families could be left without the help they urgently need,” he added.
China to send special envoy to Iran and the Gulf
China said Monday it plans to send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters the envoy would focus on easing tensions and promoting regional stability.
The Gulf region “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict,” Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said on Monday, according to a readout of their meeting.
The move comes as China seeks to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region, which it depends on for a large share of its oil.
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two men in southern Gaza early Monday, according to Nasser Hospital, where their bodies were taken. One strike killed a man in his home; the other killed a man in a tent.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Major fighting between Israel and Hamas largely halted under the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes on Gaza that it says target militants, though the strikes regularly kill or injure women and children. Israel says Hamas uses civilians as human shields.
About 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, bringing the overall death toll to more than 74,500, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

articles.title_orig: Long March leaves its footprints in British libraries
articles.title_zh: Long March leaves its footprints in British libraries
articles.content_orig:
Xinhua |
          Updated: 2026-11-03 08:54
LONDON — In a reading room at the British Library, a blue stamp dated Jan 27, 1937, appears inside a book written by a British missionary who witnessed part of China's Long March.
Nearly 90 years later, the book offers a glimpse into how the extraordinary journey of the Chinese Red Army reached readers thousands of miles away.
As this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, libraries and archives across Britain, along with the recollections of a writer who retraced the historic route, offer fresh perspectives on a journey that helped shape modern China.
At London's Marx Memorial Library, founded in 1933, two early publications shed light on how the Chinese Red Army was portrayed to British readers.
One is Edgar Snow's Red Star Over China, published in Britain in 1937. Its orange-red cover bears the words "LEFT BOOK CLUB EDITION" and "NOT FOR SALE TO THE PUBLIC".
Snow's account introduced Western readers to the CPC, its leaders and the extraordinary hardships endured by Red Army soldiers during the Long March.
Another is Agnes Smedley's China's Red Army Marches, published in London in 1936. Focusing on the Red Army's activities before its historic journey, the book describes villagers making shoes for soldiers and farmers delivering rice to support them.
One passage even reproduces a revolutionary song, complete with musical notation, preserving the voices of Chinese soldiers in a book published thousands of miles away.
The British Library also holds a 1937 edition of Snow's book bearing a stamp from the former India Office Library dated Oct 30, 1937.
Contemporary British newspapers also reflected growing interest in the Red Army. On Oct 19, 1937, the Edinburgh Evening News published a review of Snow's book, devoting a section specifically to the Long March.
Together, these publications offered British readers accounts of the soldiers' experiences, their daily lives and the circumstances surrounding their remarkable journey, bringing distant events in China into view for the British public.
At the University of East Anglia in Norwich, eastern England, three archival boxes preserve the story of Alfred Bosshardt, a British missionary who accompanied the Red Army through parts of southwestern China.
Bosshardt's experiences were later recounted in The Restraining Hand, published in Britain in 1936, making him one of the earliest Western eyewitnesses to record aspects of the Long March.
The university's collection contains hundreds of items, including correspondence, photographs, newspaper cuttings and audiovisual recordings. Many were collected by British journalist and writer Anthony Grey, who helped bring Bosshardt's story to a wider audience.
Despite their different beliefs, Bosshardt developed considerable respect for the Red Army soldiers, particularly for their discipline and determination.
He recalled that soldiers were instructed to respect villagers, pay for food and compensate residents for damaged property. During breaks from their arduous journey, young soldiers sang songs, wrestled and shared moments of laughter.
Bosshardt also admired Red Army commander Xiao Ke, with whom he later renewed contact. Their friendship continued for decades, forming a remarkable personal link between Britain and China.
Nearly seven decades after the Long March, British-based Chinese writer Sun Shuyun spent 14 months retracing the odyssey. Traveling through remote villages, she interviewed surviving Red Army veterans and their families in an effort to understand the people behind the historical narrative.
For Sun, who studied history at the University of Oxford, the journey became one of the most unforgettable experiences of her life.
In East China's Jiangxi province, she met an elderly woman who had persuaded her newlywed husband to join the Red Army. He never returned. Nearly 70 years later, she was still waiting for him.
In Northwest China's Gansu province, Sun interviewed a former female Red Army soldier whose life had been marked by poverty, captivity and hardship.
The elderly woman welcomed Sun into her home, wrapped her in thick blankets and prepared a meal unusually rich in salt. Her adopted daughter explained that salt had been extremely scarce during the Long March, leaving the woman with a lifelong habit of cherishing it.
Recalling these encounters at her London home, Sun was moved to tears.
She said the Long March demonstrated the CPC's organizational strength and leadership and laid an important foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
"The Long March is one of the most important events in modern Chinese history," she said, adding that its legacy continues to resonate with China's development today.
Sun stressed that the choices and sacrifices of ordinary people, whose experiences could sometimes be overlooked in historical narratives, deserve to be remembered and passed down to future generations.
From the hardships of revolutionary struggle to the achievements of modernization, the Chinese people have continued to undertake new journeys requiring courage and perseverance, she said.
The great spirit of the Long March "will always deserve to be remembered", Sun added.

articles.title_orig: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
articles.title_zh: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
articles.content_orig:
The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.
John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.
While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack .
The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.
"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.
Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.
Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.
During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.
Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.
Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.
Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.
Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.
As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."
It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

New Trainer profile backgrounds, private Max Battle groups, exclusive Research bonuses, and avatar rewards arrive ahead of GO Wild Area 2026.
Pokémon GO has revealed a fresh batch of details for GO Wild Area 2026 , including the ability to show Pokémon backgrounds on Trainer profiles (yes!!!) , private Dynamax Battle groups, new Special Research bonuses, and several avatar items.
The updates arrive just ahead of GO Wild Area: Mexico City and GO Wild Area: Sendai , which take place from November 6–8, 2026 . The adventure continues worldwide with GO Wild Area: Global on November 14–15, 2026 .
Here is everything new that Trainers should know before the event begins.
Starting with GO Wild Area 2026, Trainers will be able to display their Buddy Pokémon’s Location Background or Special Background on their Trainer profile. These backgrounds will also be visible to friends, giving Trainers a new way to show off Pokémon caught during special events and memorable adventures.
The feature will roll out in stages:
Additional Special Backgrounds will be supported in the future.
The feature unlocks according to each Trainer’s local time. Friends will not be able to see your Buddy Pokémon’s background until the feature has reached its scheduled unlock time in their own time zone.
One of the biggest gameplay improvements arriving with GO Wild Area is the ability to join Dynamax Battles privately .
Previously, entering a Max Battle lobby would automatically match Trainers with other participants. Starting with GO Wild Area 2026, Trainers will have two options when joining a battle:
This should make it easier for coordinated groups to tackle difficult Max Battles without being automatically matched with other players.
The change arrives just in time for Gigantamax Duraludon, Dynamax Dialga, and Dynamax Palkia , all of which are featured during GO Wild Area 2026.
For more information about their appearances, check out our GO Wild Area 2026: Global guide .
Ticket-holding Trainers participating in GO Wild Area: Global will receive a branching Special Research story starting on November 14, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. local time .
Trainers must choose between researching Steel-type or Dragon-type Pokémon. Each path awards a corresponding in-game medal and unlocks special bonuses for catching mighty Pokémon of that type.
Trainers who earn the Steel Scholar medal will unlock:
Trainers who earn the Dragon Defender medal will unlock:
The bonuses activate after claiming the corresponding medal , rather than immediately upon choosing a Research path.
Both sets of bonuses expire when GO Wild Area: Global ends on November 15, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. local time .
Unlike Global participants, ticket-holding Trainers attending Sendai or Mexico City will have the opportunity to earn both medals through their in-person event Special Research, unlocking both sets of bonuses until the conclusion of the Global event.
Several new avatar customization options have been revealed, including free GO Pass rewards, paid items, and a Special Research reward.
The following items will be available through GO Pass: Into the Wild :
GO Pass: Into the Wild runs from November 9 at 10:00 a.m. until November 15 at 6:00 p.m. local time .
Trainers have until November 17, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time to claim their unlocked rewards.
Three additional avatar items will be available for purchase during the event:
These items will remain available in the in-game shop after GO Wild Area concludes.
Ticket-holding Trainers who complete their event Special Research during the in-person GO Wild Area events or GO Wild Area: Global will receive an exclusive new avatar pose .
There is also good news for collectors!
Pokémon caught using GO Safari Balls can now be transferred from Pokémon GO to Pokémon HOME.
Once transferred, their GO Safari Ball will appear as a Strange Ball in Pokémon HOME.
This means Pokémon caught during GO Wild Area using these special Poké Balls are no longer excluded from Pokémon HOME transfers simply because of the Ball they were caught in.
Starting with the Into the Wild event , Trainers will be able to activate select Adventure Effects while waiting in a Raid or Max Battle lobby.
This includes Adventure Effects associated with:
Instead of activating an Adventure Effect before joining a lobby, Trainers can prepare their bonuses while assembling their battle group.
Ticket-holding Trainers attending the in-person GO Wild Area events in Sendai and Mexico City will receive early access to this functionality.
Trainers attending the in-person events can now preview the official event maps to help plan their routes, stops, and activities. The maps and location information are available on the official event pages:
Official event pages: Sendai • Tohoku | Mexico City
Additional event ticket add-ons are also still available for eligible attendees. These provide various gameplay bonuses, additional gameplay days, and merchandise preorder options.
Ticket add-on bonuses are active from November 6 through November 8, 2026 , allowing eligible Trainers to benefit throughout the in-person event weekend.

articles.title_orig: Iran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Iran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
With little transparency from Washington and warmongering from Tehran, people across the Middle East have been left anxious and confused, scanning for signals on whether the conflict between Iran and the United States will reignite.
“The mood has definitely shifted,” a 36-year-old American living in Saudi Arabia told CNN. She plans to leave before Tuesday’s US midterm elections, after which US President Donald Trump has hinted renewed fighting is possible.
“People are more cautious in general, and it feels like a waiting game to see what happens,” she added.
At homes and workplaces across Gulf Arab countries, questions are swirling. Residents are searching for clues that could help them plan for school closures or travel disruptions.
The war began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. It entered its eighth month this week with both sides still locked in a stubborn stalemate, neither making progress diplomatically nor able to break the military impasse.
Trump has offered little clarity on his endgame, oscillating between threats of further strikes and openness to possible diplomacy. Iran has tried to project its own deterrence, claiming it now possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before. Mediation is continuing, but a breakthrough would depend on at least one side breaching its own red lines.
Trump wrote on social media this month that Washington “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” The president neither ruled out nor confirmed that strikes would resume afterward, which is part of the reason for the ongoing nerves.
Trump also spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday. The contents of the call were unclear, though Axios, which first reported it, said the conversation concerned Iran.
Asked Sunday about his conversation with Netanyahu, Trump provided no details, saying only that he “had a very good talk” with the prime minister.
“The US has been actively feeding into this regionwide sense of anxiety as it keeps signaling that another round of escalation might be imminent,” Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow for Middle East policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told CNN. “But it’s becoming difficult to distinguish pressure tactics from genuine signals.”
Adding to a sense that escalation could be imminent, Netanyahu, who partnered with the US in attacking Iran and has been pushing for new strikes, will remain in office despite losing his majority in the recent elections. Negotiations to form a new government in Israel look set to begin in earnest next week, but election results suggest it will be difficult for opposition parties to oust Netanyahu quickly, if at all.
Without clarity, residents in the region often rely on hearsay or search social media for reports on troop movements to determine whether a US strike is imminent.
Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have also intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built up large stockpiles of new weapons, a tactic designed to induce fear among Washington’s allies in the region.
A senior security official in Tehran told CNN that Iran will try to target infrastructure beyond oil facilities in the region, including AI, and warned that if the conflict resumes, it will be a long “war of surprises.” On Saturday, Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered a response “without geographical limitations” to any new threat, an apparent effort to present a leader still yet to be seen in public as playing an active role in military preparations.
Foreign workers drawn to wealthy Gulf Arab states by economic opportunities and a tax-free lifestyle have for decades lived in relative stability in a region mired in conflict. That sense of security was shattered this year after the US and Israel launched the war, prompting Tehran to fire unprecedented barrages of ballistic missiles and drones onto Arab cities, disrupting schools, travel and business and causing multiple casualties.
Yet, despite the war, many residents stayed put, telling CNN they feel confident under the protection of well-armed regional militaries. Practical concerns remain, though.
“I’m actively trying not to think about that happening again because I really don’t want another winter with strikes,” Michelle, a 36-year-old American resident of Abu Dhabi, told CNN. “I’ve always felt safe here… but I’m more concerned that our lives will have to change again.”
This month, people were surprised to learn that families of US diplomats have begun leaving discreetly, with the departures becoming known only after their children started saying goodbye to classmates at school. Many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out at the height of the Iran war in March, making the exits feel like a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu.
Fueling anxiety among residents are reports of thousands of US troops being dispatched to the region, as reported by the Associated Press.
In Saudi Arabia, where major events have already been canceled and offices closed with staff working remotely after the Iran-allied Houthi rebels intensified strikes, residents told CNN they were concerned that a return to war could increase pressure on a country already embroiled in conflict along its southern border.
“My neighbors and friends are bunkering for November but starting to get concerned about flight disruptions over the holidays,” said a 36-year-old American in Saudi Arabia, comparing it to the Covid era. “A lot of offices have moved to virtual or have reduced staff and remote learning is in place.”
Elsewhere in the region, other international gatherings remain on track, though the risk remains that they could be disrupted if the US launches strikes in the coming week.
In Abu Dhabi, where no attacks have been recorded since May, two US oil firms canceled plans for their executives to attend one of the region’s biggest energy conferences, citing security concerns, Reuters reported. The event will proceed as scheduled next week with “strong” US participation and more than 120 American exhibiting companies, the organizer, DMG, told Reuters.
The conference is expected to host nearly 240,000 people, according to the organizers.
In Bahrain, one of the worst-hit countries by Iran this year, people said they still felt the psychological impact of the war.
“There is still that traumatic effect,” 21-year-old Fawaz told CNN. “When you hear the bombings, it’s kind of like you feel it in your hearts and it’s hard to sleep at night, especially when there are bombings outside.”
“A lot of people have become used to it by now, but it’s still very scary,” he added.
Despite growing anxiety over the possible resumption of war, there has been a flurry of quiet diplomacy over the past week.
US Vice President JD Vance sent Iran’s top security official Mohsen Rezaei a letter, which the Islamic Republic is reviewing, according to Iranian media. Trump has claimed the letter related to an Iranian request for medical supplies, but it has raised hopes that a diplomatic breakthrough could still be possible.
Iranian officials are in Qatar for talks, a Qatari official said. Qatar has played a prominent role in mediating, but the official added there was no US delegation present Saturday.
On Monday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the ball is “entirely in the US’ court,” as “exchanges of messages” between Washington and Tehran were ongoing, according to Iran’s state news agency, IRNA. Baghaei doubled down on Tehran’s demand that “no agreement can be reached,” nor the key Strait of Hormuz reopened, as long as the US naval blockade on Iranian ports remains.

articles.title_orig: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.title_zh: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.content_orig:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.
“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Still, some analysts see a narrow opening.
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

articles.title_zh: Gulf Economies, Torn by War in Iran, Desperately Need a Return to Normal
articles.content_orig:
Riyadh Air, Saudi Arabia’s aspiring luxury carrier, is busing international passengers to and from an alternate airport four and a half hours from its hub, which was damaged in strikes.
The marquee Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year.
The headquarters of the state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco were struck, as was a critical pipeline. Ships running the gantlet in the vital Strait of Hormuz are still in Iran’s cross hairs and catching fire from missile and drone attacks. It is a particularly tense time right now, with a heightened risk of escalation of the war.
Throughout the Persian Gulf, the war in Iran, now at the start of its ninth month, and the conflict that has erupted in Yemen are taxing the region’s ability to conduct business as normal.
This week could bring a fresh test. The energy conference ADIPEC, featuring executives and government ministers from around the world, began in Abu Dhabi on Monday. At least one prominent industry leader, Darren Woods, the chief executive of Exxon Mobil, decided not to attend because of security concerns in the region, according to a person familiar with his thinking who was not authorized to speak to the media.
The event’s organizers said in a statement that “high-level participation is very strong” but did not comment on the reasons for Mr. Woods’s withdrawal.
Economic growth across the Gulf Cooperation Council, a regional bloc of Arab states, will tumble by 5 percent this year, according to the International Monetary Fund. Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar are expected to suffer double-digit contractions, linked to their near-total dependence on the besieged Strait of Hormuz to sell their energy products to the world.

articles.title_orig: MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes, watchdog writes
articles.title_zh: MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes, watchdog writes
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
In less than four years, the MTA could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue, according to a new analysis from the Citizens Budget Commission, which recommends cutting the workforce to close the gap.
The budget watchdog recommends sweeping job cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete. The budget commission suggested the MTA allow its trains to run with just one worker, instead of two.
Train lines that have new computer-based signals, like the L and the 7, are already fully automated, as are the announcements on the trains. While the conductor opens and closes the train doors, the operator has few other duties, which include hitting a button every 20 seconds to signal they are alert. The budget commission cited the operator’s limited responsibilities as a sign the job could be cut with no impact to service.
Eliminating operator jobs on the L and 7 lines could save $36.5 million a year, according to the report . If the agency moved to phase out two people operating trains across the system, it could save $500 million a year.
The agency is in the process of installing new signals on other lines like the A, C, E, F, G, M and R lines. For now, those lines still require two people to run the trains.
The suggestion from the Citizens Budget Commission comes at a sensitive time as Transport Workers Union Local 100 negotiates a contract with the MTA for its 40,000 subway and bus workers. The MTA is expected to release its financial plan for next year in the coming weeks, which will include a 4% fare and toll increase. The board will vote on that plan in December.
“The same recommendations have been coming down for dozens of years, so there's nothing new about it,” said Transport Workers Union of America President John Samuelsen. “It's essentially a recommendation to balance alleged deficits that the MTA has off the backs of working people.”
Last year, the state legislature tried to enshrine a requirement of two MTA workers on each train into law, but Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill , leaving open the possibility that one-person train operations could happen in the future.
“Legislatively mandated staffing prevents the MTA from modernizing — as technology and best practices continue to improve — and realizing the efficiency and financial benefits,” the Citizens Budget Commission's report argues.
The Citizens Budget Commission acknowledges the MTA has become more efficient in recent years, saving a reported $576 million this year through what the agency calls “operating efficiencies.” But the report argues that without cutting labor and healthcare costs, the MTA faces a $300 million budget gap next year that will grow to $900 million by 2030. The budget commission estimates its recommended reforms could save $2.5 billion annually.
Other recommendations include streamlining fare collection on the commuter railroads by checking tickets prior to boarding, reducing the need for someone to walk through the train. The Citizens Budget Commission argues cutting more than 1,000 jobs on Metro-North and the Long Island Rail Road could save $380 million annually.
The report also recommended MTA retirees pay more in healthcare premiums, which could bring in an additional $315 million a year.
Samuelsen countered that many laborers, ironworkers, track workers, and crane operators in the MTA get paid less than their peers in the private sector, but accept that because of the generous retirement benefits.
"The CBC is right to note that we've made extraordinary progress in securing hundreds of millions of dollars in new recurring operational efficiencies," MTA spokesperson Mitch Schwartz wrote in a statement. He did not address the proposal to eliminate jobs.
Stephen Nessen covers transportation. Since 2008 he has reported on everything from Occupy Wall Street, the rebuilding of the World Trade Center site, Hurricane Sandy, to Trump’s campaign for president. His transportation reporting has taken him everywhere from the MTA’s secret Rail Control Center to the gleaming subways of Seoul. Got a tip? Email [email protected] .

articles.title_orig: Frantic Binance Hackers Created Windfall for Fast Crypto Traders
articles.title_zh: Frantic Binance Hackers Created Windfall for Fast Crypto Traders
articles.content_orig:
Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever .
In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets.
"Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.
Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance. Roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets were frozen, according to Binance. Freezing crypto funds allows certain issuers to block the transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world.
The hacker group believed to be responsible for the attack, known as "TraderTraitor," was converting most of the stolen assets into Ethereum in a move to hide their tracks, the FBI said Saturday. TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds. By early Sunday morning, it said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount.

articles.title_orig: Marvell, Lumentum tout historic $115B deal to create ‘category leader’ in AI connectivity
articles.title_zh: Marvell, Lumentum tout historic $115B deal to create ‘category leader’ in AI connectivity
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston detail their record-breaking merger and how their ‘shared vision’ will create a category leader in AI connectivity on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
Marvell Technology chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said the chipmaker’s historic $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum is a "once in a generation’ opportunity to unite two of the most dominating companies in the AI boom and create a "category leader."
Appearing alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston on "The Claman Countdown," Murphy detailed the companies’ record-breaking merger on Monday, predicting that the transaction will cement Marvell’s position at the forefront of AI connectivity.
"It's very rare that you can find two companies of the caliber of Lumentum and Marvell that are number one in their respective areas that find a moment in time where you can combine and create a category leader in a new category," he told anchor Liz Claman.
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD
The race to build AI infrastructure is accelerating as concerns grow over centralized technological power. (Noah Berger / Getty Images)
"This AI connectivity is going to be as consequential as… the compute category, or the memory category, the fab category, and the IP licensing category."
Murphy's comments follow the announcement of Marvell’s agreement to acquire Lumentum in a landmark $115 billion transaction, marking the largest merger between two publicly traded companies. The deal will unite two massive AI enablers, equipped with electrical and optical expertise, to address connectivity requirements for next-generation AI infrastructure .
MASSIVE AI BOOM PUTS ONE OF AMERICA’S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS ON PATH TO DOUBLE IN SIZE, CEO SAYS
"Both companies.are executing phenomenally well. And what we see, Liz, is a multiplying effect, where we're gonna do much better together in two years than we would on a standalone basis," Hurlston predicted.
Under the terms of the all-stock agreement, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each share held, according to Marvell’s announcement.
"It’s really a historic day for the two companies," Murphy said. "We're putting together basically the best-in-class leader in AI connectivity technology for semiconductors with the leader in photonics. And it is something that hasn't been done before."
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy (Right) appeared alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston (Left) on "The Claman Countdown" on Monday. (Left (Takaaki Iwabu/Bloomberg via Getty Images), Right (Lam Yik Fei/Bloomberg via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
Marvell designs artificial intelligence chips and technology that powers data centers , while Lumentum designs lasers and other optical components that use light to transmit data between chips and servers.
Murphy said Lumentum and Marvell, both headquartered in Northern California, have a "shared vision" and detailed how he believes the two tech companies will work better together than apart.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
"Together, because of the additional opportunity we see with each other, there's an opportunity to really outperform as a combined company," the Marvell CEO said.
Murphy, who said the merger has received "tremendous support" from hyperscalers, told FOX Business that he expects "significant" revenue synergies and other benefits once the companies are joined together.
AI chip giant Nvidia is a strategic investor in both Lumentum, which has a market value of around $76 billion, and Marvell, with a value of roughly $172 billion.
The Marvell-Lumentum deal has garnered "super positive" feedback from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Hurlston said. (Getty )
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Hurlston told FOX Business that Murphy discussed the potential Lumentum acquisition with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang early in the process, adding that reaction from Nvidia has been "super positive."
"Nvidia is invested in Marvell, Nvidia is invested in Lumentum. We think we can actually bring a lot more product to bear to Nvidia a lot more quickly in this combination," Hurlston said.

articles.content_orig:
Pharmalot Columnist, Senior Writer
Ed’s stories explore prescription drug pricing, affordability and access, as well issues surrounding patents, litigation, and legislation. He is also the author of the morning Pharmalittle newsletter and the afternoon Pharmalot newsletter .
After months of anticipation, the Food and Drug Administration gave tentative approval to Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories to make a generic version of a groundbreaking HIV prevention medicine , a key step in widening access for dozens of low- and middle-income countries.
The company, one of the world’s largest generic drugmakers, plans to start shipping the medicine next month as part of an effort propelled, in part, by several global health organizations to ensure the drug becomes available in lower-income countries as quickly as possible. The annual cost per person will be $40, comparable to daily tablets.
Known as lenacapavir, the injectable drug is widely seen as a game-changing tool for eradicating HIV because it offers virtually complete protection against contracting the virus with just one administration every six months. The brand-name version, which is known as Yetzugo in the U.S., is marketed by Gilead Sciences and was approved by the FDA last year .

articles.title_orig: Two Chinese Nationals Receive Less Than Three Years Prison Time for Spying on US Navy
articles.title_zh: Two Chinese Nationals Receive Less Than Three Years Prison Time for Spying on US Navy
articles.content_orig:
The pair was accused of gathering information about U.S. military personnel and facilitating secret cash payments.
Two Chinese nationals have been sentenced to 30 months in prison for acting as illegal agents of the People’s Republic of China after conducting surveillance operations targeting U.S. Navy personnel and military facilities.
Their charges are conspiring to act as agents of the PRC government and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General.
One of the convicted criminals, Liren “Ryan” Lai, was arrested in Houston last year.
According to court documents, Lai and co-defendant Yuance Chen of Oregon began acting as agents under a Chinese intelligence officer with PRC’s Ministry of State Security in 2021.
Authorities alleged that the pair photographed U.S. military personnel and facilities, Navy recruiting offices, and naval installations in Washington and California.
They also reportedly attempted to recruit other potential MSS members from the U.S. military.
“Chen and Lai operated as illegal agents for the Chinese government on U.S. soil, carrying out clandestine intelligence work that included making covert payments, collecting sensitive military information, and attempting to recruit American service members,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
Their activities included secret “dead drop” cash payments in exchange for intelligence related to the national security of the U.S.
A dead drop of $10,000 was reportedly sent to Chen. The MSS also directed Lai to travel to Phoenix in 2025 to facilitate a cash payment of $20,000.
An unsealed federal affidavit cited an incident that involved Chen surveilling the Naval Special Warfare Command in San Diego, which oversees Navy SEALs.
The pair were arrested on June 27, 2025, in a coordinated FBI counterintelligence and law enforcement operation.
A federal grand jury in the Northern District of California returned an indictment charging both defendants with conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the attorney general and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification.
Both pleaded guilty and received sentences of 30 months in prison and three years of supervised release.
“Lai’s and Chen’s activities, undertaken at the direction of the PRC, were extensive and brazen. The National Security Division is committed to holding accountable anyone who aids or abets such espionage efforts,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.
Rozhavsky noted that while “The Chinese government’s efforts to infiltrate our armed forces demonstrate just how far it will go to threaten U.S. national security,” the country has “underestimated the FBI’s commitment to thwarting its illegal activity and holding its agents accountable.”
“Let this sentencing serve as a clear warning: If you attempt to jeopardize the safety and security of our service members, our citizens, or our nation, justice will find you,” added Rozhavsky.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Investors Push for Cautious Valuation Closer to $1.5 Trillion
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Investors Push for Cautious Valuation Closer to $1.5 Trillion
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.
The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.
Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.
During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.
The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.
As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds , and quarterly reports from Microsoft , Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.
The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows , causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.
In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.
"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.
The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut .
Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors . The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.
"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.
The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).
RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.
To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.
Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”
When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.
But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):
In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.
For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.
However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”
Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.
Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

articles.title_orig: Rivian Stock Can Rise More Than 30%. The R2 Isn’t Just for ‘Tesla Switchers.’
articles.title_zh: Rivian Stock Can Rise More Than 30%. The R2 Isn’t Just for ‘Tesla Switchers.’
articles.content_orig:
Rivian Automotive beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors will lead it to profitability.
Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Shares of Rivian were up roughly 7% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%
The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.
The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.
Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.
The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said.
Rivian delivered a record 19,248 units from July through September. The company does not disclose deliveries by vehicle.
The EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.
Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.
The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.
Also on Thursday, Rivian reiterated that it expects the R2, a smaller and less expensive sibling to its current luxury R1S SUV, to have a positive gross margin by the end of the year. CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve overall profitability.
"That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," Scaringe told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview Thursday. "We're going to see that through the end of the quarter and the unit economics will continue to grow … into Q1 of next year as well."
Rivian on Thursday said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.

articles.title_orig: Russia kills at least 24 in horrific bombing on Ukraine school
articles.title_zh: Russia kills at least 24 in horrific bombing on Ukraine school
articles.content_orig:
At least 24 people were killed after Russian forces bombed a Ukrainian school on Monday in what President Volodymyr Zelensky slammed as a barbaric “double-tap” strike.
Ukraine’s emergency service confirmed that the Komyshuvakha school targeted in the strike was a building used for distributing humanitarian aid, with two of its rescue workers among the dead.
“After the first air strike, there was a repeat strike with nine more bombs, directly on the shelter where people were gathered,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
“The Russians could not have been unaware that every week residents who have remained in Komyshuvakha were receiving assistance right there,” he continued.
“This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of de-escalation , any real justice,” Zelensky added.
Monday’s strike occurred in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, where officials said that 27 people were still missing in the attack.
Rescue teams are currently trying to reach residents who are believed to still be trapped under the rubble, Zaporizhzhia police said.
The threat of repeated Russian attacks in the region has also complicated the search and rescue efforts, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi noted.
Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin declared Nov. 3 a day of mourning for the victims of the attack.
The Russian military has yet to comment on the deadly airstrike.
The deadly attack came just a day after a localized cease-fire secured by first lady Melania Trump in Russian-occupied Oleshky.
“After the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelensky said.
“With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings,” he added.
