articles.title_orig: Review: Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (Switch 2) - Perfectly Playable, Despite Drawbacks
articles.title_zh: Review: Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (Switch 2) - Perfectly Playable, Despite Drawbacks
articles.content_orig:
Though the genre has evolved and deepened over time, gacha games have historically not been praised for their depth and complexity, often being criticised for being thinly veiled gambling machines. People were understandably incredulous, then, when Shift Up — the studio behind Goddess of Victory: Nikke — announced in 2019 that it would pursue a AAA passion project called Stellar Blade . Even more were then shocked a few years later when this wildly different, ambitious project turned out to be a pretty solidly made action game.
Stellar Blade has now been ported to Switch 2 (along with some cheeky new cosmetic Bayonetta DLC), bringing this titillating and gripping action experience to the Nintendo audience. It hasn’t made the transition to more modest hardware completely unscathed, but this is nonetheless a solidly enjoyable and thrilling adventure that deserves a spot in your library.
The narrative is set in the distant, post-apocalypse future, when our planet has been overrun by monstrous creatures called Naytibas. Some humans escaped after losing the war and established a space-based orbital colony called…the Colony…from which occasional squadrons of elite super-soldiers are deployed to attempt to regain a foothold on Earth.
Protagonist Eve is a member of one of these squads and the prologue opens with her landing mission, a violent meatgrinder reminiscent of the Omaha Beach scene in Saving Private Ryan in which she’s seemingly the sole warrior who survives. Aided by a mysterious man who saved her, Eve sets out to track down the Alpha Naytiba and hopefully notch a win for the humans.
It’s a decently entertaining story, but one which feels a little surface-level in many ways. Characters — Eve included — lack depth and converse in a stilted way that sounds as if they’re quoting lines at each other, and some of the later plot twists are the sort of thing that you can see coming a mile away. Yet there’s just enough lore here to keep you interested in the setting and Eve’s ongoing journey and occasional moments of levity help to keep things from feeling too dour.
Any disappointment with the storytelling is quickly forgotten by the thrill of combat, which feels like a cross between a Soulslike and a character action game as Eve deftly combos enemies with her athletic acrobatics and expert sword strikes.
Enemies hit hard and fast and can easily stunlock you, meaning that even a single average foe can take quite a large chunk out of your health bar if you're not paying careful attention and multiple foes at once can rapidly overwhelm Eve due to limited mobility and crowd control options.
Along with the usual combos you can string together with light and heavy attacks, Eve also has a variety of limited-use Beta Skills she can use to turn the tide in her favour. You build up Beta Energy from attacks and perfectly timed blocks or parries, and this energy can then be burned mid-combo to either bolster an attack or use a flashy guard-breaking attack that can put the enemy on the back foot. This system adds a nice bit of room for player skill expression, as you can find some creative ways to weave together combos and Beta Skills to positively melt foes.
Though even common enemies can put you to the test in certain configurations, this combat system really sings when you get to one of the many cinematic boss fights against powerful, grotesque monsters. These act as occasional hard skill checks that will forcibly teach you deeper knowledge of combat mechanics as you carefully study their movesets for brief gaps and learn (often across multiple failed attempts) how to best exploit those gaps with your available tools.
Eve thus feels both all-powerful and vulnerable at the same time, which lends combat encounters a thrilling and electric feel as you oscillate between slicing enemies to ribbons with practised cinematic flair and getting absolutely folded when you mis-time a dodge. Practice makes perfect, and there's lots of satisfaction that comes from progressing across the hours and going up against increasingly more complicated and dangerous foes with sharpened reflexes and skill.
Yet progress happens in more ways than just raw skill development - there are also some light RPG elements that allow you to slowly shape Eve's build over time. Not only can you use skill points to unlock and power up new combat abilities and Beta Skills, but you can also improve stats like max health and attack through finding collectibles in the environment.
Gear can also be found and crafted to give Eve certain passive buffs, allowing you to get more value out of the playstyle you generally choose. These RPG mechanics help to soften some of the harder edges of the often unforgiving combat system, giving you meaningful ways to progress over time even if you struggle greatly with losing battles to enemies.
World and level design initially follows traditional Soulslike tropes, consisting of lots of claustrophobic halls and labyrinthine paths that often loop back on each other with unlocked doors and ladders that lead back to the nearest checkpoint. While the critical path is usually obvious and easy to follow, there are often a handful of side areas to explore along the way rife with more platforming gauntlets, challenging enemy placements and extra upgrades and goodies. This design does a great job of rewarding exploration while keeping you moving forward.
Then, roughly six or so hours in, things change up with the sudden introduction of a medium-sized open-world area, filled with quests, collectibles, and points of interest to scour. Travelling between this area and a nearby hub has both gameplay and narrative benefits, as you complete quests and bounties to progress various side storylines for NPCs living there and find increasingly better gear and unlockables as quest and exploration rewards.
It admittedly seems at first like a weird left turn after the opening hours set very different expectations, but ultimately feels like a worthy addition to the gameplay loop. And even after its introduction, there are plenty of returns to the more focused and level-based Soulslike design, which balances out the free but occasionally meandering levels and quests that can come with the open world.
Graphics look decent, but not exceptional, due in part to both the overall art direction and the Switch 2’s relatively modest hardware. Some of the vistas of the ruined Earth can be quite nice to look at from afar, but there’s a lot of muted colours utilised as you trawl through tunnels, sewers, deserts, and destroyed office buildings. Environments thus tend to blend together and often lack visually interesting landmarks or set pieces, which can make the sections more focused on exploration a little more dull.
Meanwhile, the game outputs at 720p handheld and 1080p docked, which can lead to visuals that look even more muddy due to the upscaling artifacting and relatively low internal resolutions.
Regarding performance, everything technically runs at 60fps, but there's a pretty massive caveat with that claim: this frame rate is only accomplished through frame generation. Practically speaking, this means that there's a significant amount of input lag despite the visuals themselves appearing to animate smoothly. For a game this focused on quick reaction times and granular movement, that input lag can be a death knell and does noticeably reduce the playability of this port.
However, there is an option in the settings to turn this off and reduce the game to what appears to be closer to 40fps, which feels like a much more acceptable compromise. Controls are quite a bit more responsive here, while the frame rate is noticeably smoother than 30fps. There are some drops that can still happen when panning the camera around in larger areas, but it doesn’t overly affect the playability of combat encounters and this becomes less of an issue in the many smaller environments.
All this is to say, Stellar Blade is a game

articles.title_orig: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.title_zh: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.content_orig:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has scrapped plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for permanent settlement.
Mahmood had proposed doubling the wait for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait.
But following a backlash from several Labour MPs, Mahmood revised the policy and care workers who earn at least £25,000 a year and arrived in the UK before May 2025 would continue to qualify after five years.
The Conservatives said Mahmood's "U-turn" would cost taxpayers billions of pounds.
ILR, also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.
Last November, Mahmood announced plans to delay settlements in response to concerns over the number of people approaching eligibility, in the wake of record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Conservative government, nicknamed the "Boriswave".
Asked by the BBC whether she had u-turned on her earlier promises, she replied "I don't accept that", adding that some 500,000 people in the UK "will not now settle at five years".
"They will have to wait longer before they can achieve settlement in this country, and I've come to a fair resolution for care workers," she said.
The Home Office has said its figures show net migration - the difference between those entering and leaving the country - added 2.6m people to the UK population between 2021 and 2024.
The department estimates that between 2026 and 2030 between 1.3m and 2.2m people will settle in the UK, adding its central estimate has increased to 1.9m.
The home secretary faced criticism for proposing to apply the changes to migrant workers already in the UK, with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner previously saying this would "change the goalposts" .
Several Labour MPs also described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and  warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.
Making a statement to the House of Commons, Mahmood said settlement "should not be automatic, it should be earned".
The changes will move those earning less than £50,000 a year onto a 10-year path to settlement status, unless they are exempt.
Mahmood also told MPs the government would provide a five-year path to settlement for care workers who "answered our call when we needed them" following the Covid-19 pandemic.
Mahmood said: "Those who earn £25,000 a year working in the social care sector, which was the condition of their visa, will therefore be able to settle on their existing five-year path."
She added those care workers who did not meet the conditions of their visa could apply for another five-year visa and seek settlement after that.
Mahmood said: "Our changes ensure those who are net contributors are encouraged to come to this country and stay here."
She added: "As a result, the Department for Work and Pensions estimates that our reforms will reduce the benefits bill by billions of pounds."
The original version of the plans announced by Mahmood last year would have delayed 799,000 people from gaining permanent residency. Under the updated plans announced on Monday, that number would drop to 517,000.
One of those affected was Ashfak Juned, a Bangladeshi chef working in Birmingham, who told the BBC he was  "crying" when he heard his wait for settled status would now last until 2033.
The home secretary also confirmed a number of groups would see their settlement path remain as it is today - including Hong Kong British nationals overseas, armed forces members, people with a British connection and those on legacy routes including the Windrush scheme.
The Refugee Council's Imran Hussain said the plans for those who had travelled to the UK illegally or by small boat and do not work or study to wait 30 years for ILR were "unfair and unworkable".
"The fairest reforms would be making fast and good quality asylum decisions, with those refugees granted protection being helped to rebuild their lives and to contribute, and those with no right to remain helped to leave with dignity," he said.
For the Conservatives, shadow home secretary Chris Philp said opposition from Mahmood's fellow ministers and the "Labour open borders left" had resulted in the changes from Mahmood's original proposals, adding that she was "no longer running the government's immigration policy".
He highlighted figures from March in which Home Office calculations suggested 196,000 care workers and their adult dependants could settle between 2026 and 2030, at an estimated lifetime cost of £9.5bn to taxpayers.
Philp said this was the "cost of today's U-turn".
But Father of the House Sir Edward Leigh, the longest-serving male MP in the Commons, criticised his Conservative colleague for overseeing the so-called Boriswave after Brexit, where net migration peaked at nearly one million in 2023.
"Some of us don't have amnesia," he said.
Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesman Max Wilkinson said the government's reforms were "unravelling".
He added: "Viewing immigration simply as a matter of raw numbers and images of small boat arrivals is degrading this nation's ability to have the informed national discussion that we need."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Mahmood had "shown her true colours".
"She talked a big game on immigration but has u-turned at the first sign of trouble from her left wing Labour colleagues," he said.
Pointing to Home Office estimates that more than 200,000 immigrants arriving on Health and Care visas would be eligible for British citizenship before the next election, he claimed this would cost the taxpayer £50bn over their lifetimes.
He vowed to review citizenship of all those arriving on care visas from today and extend the qualifying period for citizenship to a minimum of 10 years.
Green Party MP Siân Berry said Mahmood had provided a "new obstacle course of hoops and barriers" for migrants living in the UK.
On Monday, the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank said that skilled workers and their dependants due to settle in the UK under current rules are expected to make a net lifetime contribution of around £115bn through the taxes they pay.

articles.title_orig: Oracle Is Offering $10 Billion of High-Grade Dollar Bonds
articles.title_zh: Oracle Is Offering $10 Billion of High-Grade Dollar Bonds
articles.content_orig:
Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.
While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe
articles.title_zh: New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Supermarkets across Europe were hit Monday by a new wave of apparent cyberattacks affecting fridges and freezers .
The incidents caused temperature spikes and spoiled food at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia.
They follow a cyberattack in France last month , in which, police said, hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and causing fires and food losses.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
The continent is confronting broader security fears stemming from Russia’s war in Ukraine .
The new cyberattack highlights how digital threats can increasingly affect people’s everyday lives, the European Commission said Monday.
The Ahold Delhaize supermarket chain in the Netherlands told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of an “IT incident” affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of its stores. “Our teams are working hard to fully assess the situation,” it said in an email.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of the Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops’ fridge systems were attacked. The Carrefour supermarket chain in the country said a “cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact,” affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores.
The Swedish furniture giant Ikea said its store in Mons, Belgium, was also affected.
The “cyber incident” hit the shop’s refrigeration and freezer units, according to a statement sent via email. The company said it was investigating exactly what had happened.
The store in Mons is open to customers, and none of Ikea’s other stores in Belgium have been affected, it said.
Swedish grocery retailer chain ICA also told NBC News that its systems were not affected but that it had been informed of “an incident at a small number of stores that use an external supplier and have their connectivity outside ICA’s central network.”
The incident has affected the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems, the company said in an email. “ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the incident,” it said.
The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It said it was working to discard the affected items.
The privately held grocery retail group Coop told the Swedish daily Aftonbladet that similar incidents had affected six of its stores.
In Ireland, the food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber incident had affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.
“Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue and we took immediate action,” it said in a statement. “Our investigation is ongoing.” The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and also turned up the temperature to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, public broadcaster ERR reported.
From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
Sweden’s national cybersecurity center — which said it could not speculate on who was behind the attacks — is working on several incidents affecting grocery stores across the country, the head of the center, John Billow, said Monday.
“We have in recent weeks ... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_zh: Oil prices slide in biggest drop since July on hope for more Iran talks
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: Palantir reports booming U.S. commercial revenue growth, topping government for first time
articles.title_zh: Palantir reports booming U.S. commercial revenue growth, topping government for first time
articles.content_orig:
Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools.
Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates:
Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share.
"I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople.
Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3.
U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years.
Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026.
Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability.
In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity .
"My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here."

articles.title_orig: Explorer Gadget Gets a Major Upgrade, Alongside New Quality-of-Life Updates
articles.title_zh: Explorer Gadget Gets a Major Upgrade, Alongside New Quality-of-Life Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Explorer Gadget now works while you play, alongside a redesigned catch summary, faster Pokémon appraisal, and several gameplay improvements.
The Explorer Gadget is getting a useful upgrade in Pokémon GO! Trainers can now use it to automatically catch Pokémon and spin PokéStops while actively playing the game , rather than only when Pokémon GO is running in the background.
Alongside the Explorer Gadget improvements, several quality-of-life updates have recently rolled out, including a redesigned catch summary, a dedicated Appraise button, clearer PokéStop visuals, and changes to Power Spot encounters.
Here’s what’s new and how it works.
Previously, the Explorer Gadget could automatically attempt to catch Pokémon and spin PokéStops while Pokémon GO wasn’t actively open on your device. With this update, it can now do both while you’re playing, much like a Pokémon GO Plus + accessory.
Trainers level 20 and above can activate the Explorer Gadget by tapping its icon in the top-right corner of the Map View or finding it under Key Items in the Item Bag.
When active, a pink Poké Ball icon will appear above Pokémon or PokéStops that the Explorer Gadget is attempting to interact with.
You can still catch Pokémon or spin PokéStops yourself while the Explorer Gadget is active.
Simply tap the Pokémon or PokéStop that the Gadget is targeting to take over the interaction. However, you’ll only have a limited window of time to do so once the pink Poké Ball icon appears.
There are a few important restrictions to keep in mind:
Trainers can review which Pokémon the Explorer Gadget caught and how many PokéStops it spun by opening the Explorer Gadget from the Map View or the Key Items section of the Item Bag.
If you’re unfamiliar with this feature, check out our Explorer Gadget guide for more information.
The Explorer Gadget isn’t the only thing getting attention. Pokémon GO has also rolled out several smaller gameplay and interface improvements.
The screen displayed after catching a Pokémon has been redesigned, with clearer visuals for catch rewards and bonuses. This should make it easier to see exactly what you earned from each catch.
Checking a Pokémon’s IVs is now easier! A dedicated Appraise button has been added to Pokémon summary screens, just above the Additional Options button.
This removes the need to open the Additional Options menu every time you want to appraise a Pokémon.
Visiting a Power Spot or placing a Pokémon at a Power Spot after winning a Max Battle will no longer trigger special wild encounters around the Power Spot.
According to Pokémon GO, this change is intended to improve the consistency of wild encounters for all players.
The visual rings surrounding wild Pokémon attracted by Lure Modules or encountered while exploring Routes have been updated.
Spun PokéStops now have adjusted color saturation, making them easier to distinguish from unspun PokéStops.
This is a welcome accessibility improvement, particularly for Trainers who have difficulty distinguishing between similar colors.
The visual effects surrounding Pokémon attracted by the Mystery Box or Coin Bag have also been refreshed.
These are relatively small changes individually, but together they should make everyday Pokémon GO gameplay a little more convenient.

articles.title_orig: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.title_zh: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.content_orig:
Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.
On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.
By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.
The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.
Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.
“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”
Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.
“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”
Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”
On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.
The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

articles.title_orig: Meta delays new business terms after outcry over potential web scraping of news sites
articles.title_zh: Meta delays new business terms after outcry over potential web scraping of news sites
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Meta said it was postponing the rollout of new terms for its business accounts after an outcry from media companies and open-web advocates who said the updated rules would allow the tech giant to scrape vast amounts of data and potentially build competing services.
The new rules, originally scheduled to go into effect Oct. 30, authorize Meta to use automated software such as web scrapers and bots to “index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs” associated with a business account.
The terms would have applied to all business clients, regardless of opposition, and without payment for the extracted content. Critics say Meta would have been able to use the content to potentially build products such as AI services that could compete with news publishers.
The new terms only apply to business accounts. Regular users of Meta's platforms, including Instagram and Facebook, can already have their posts scraped to train AI models as long as they are public.
Opposition to Meta's new terms is growing across Europe
On Oct. 28, a court in Norway granted a temporary injunction suspending Meta's new terms at the request of 180 Norwegian media companies, pending a full assessment of their legality.
Their case was supported by the Norwegian Media Businesses’ Association (MBL), whose member newspapers account for approximately 97% of Norwegian newspaper circulation.
“We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL chair of the board.
The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority said Oct. 30 it was starting its own investigation into the conditions.
“The CMA is concerned that Meta requiring news publishers and other content businesses to accept these terms could amount to an unlawful imposition of unfair trading conditions,” it said Friday.
Meta, however, says the terms don't change how the company uses web crawlers.
“This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites,” wrote Meta spokesman Andy Stone on X on Oct. 16.
His comments came after a report by the Nieman Journalism Lab at Harvard University, which said that as written, “the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products.” Niemen Lab said it consulted three legal experts who reviewed the terms at its request.
While there do not appear to have been any lawsuits filed in the U.S., the Association of American Publishers called on Meta to drop the new terms.
“In putting forth these onerous terms of service Meta is implicitly acknowledging that permission is required for them to use creative works to develop and improve their products,” said Maria A. Pallante, AAP president and CEO in a statement. “But at the same time this mega-corporation is abusing its dominant market power by compelling such consent from any commercial user who connects to any of their platforms.”
At some point after Nieman Lab's report, Meta removed the word “train” from the updated terms. The company says the update is not about scraping news sites.
Meta on Oct. 29 said it was listening to feedback and said for now its existing terms remain in place.
“We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” Stone posted on X.
European critics say the changes made by Meta are not sufficient
The Norwegian MBL said it wasn't satisfied with the postponement and Meta's assurances were insufficient.
“This is about people’s access to trustworthy and critical journalism,” Randi S. Øgrey, CEO of the Norwegian MBL, said in a statement. “When the financial foundations of independent news media are weakened, media diversity and the democratic public sphere are at stake.”
She said Norwegian media had three demands: Meta should commit in its new terms to respecting publishers’ reservations against scraping; using journalism in AI products should happen only after a separate, voluntary agreement and with payment; and publishers who do not sign the new terms should not be marginalized on Meta’s social platforms.
The Movement for an Open Web, the group which originally complained to the CMA, called Meta's move and the regulator's investigation a “significant win," but warned it was only the start.
“Unless the CMA and other regulators make it abundantly and quickly clear that this sort of anti-competitive landgrab is not acceptable, then we will continue to see the tech giants throwing their weight around in this way," said Tim Cowen from MOW.
The European Union executive body, the European Commission , confirmed it had discussed the proposed new terms with Meta and welcomed the postponement of their entry into force.
Spokesperson Sara Simonini said the commission was committed to ensuring that Meta’s practices comply with EU law, which prohibits a company from abusing its dominant market position and requires “gatekeeper” companies such as Meta to offer fair terms of use to businesses using their social platforms.
Simonini also said the EU executive had asked unspecified providers of AI models to give details about what training material they use, in line with the EU’s new AI Act adopted in 2024 and currently being implemented.
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

articles.title_orig: Yemen's Houthis advance to within 80 km of Aden, sources say
articles.title_zh: Yemen's Houthis advance to within 80 km of Aden, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Al-Jawf has become a new focal point in the conflict between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis, highlighting the strategic importance of the northern governorate.
A major counteroffensive has been launched by the Yemeni government army and forces loyal to it to capture the strategic heights east of the provincial capital, al-Hazm, from the Houthis.
The operations are part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched by the government last month to reverse Houthi territorial gains and restore state control in the country.
Al-Hazm has become a central part of this operation, with the city a potential launchpad for government forces against the Houthis. They have controlled the capital Sanaa and most of northern Yemen since the war broke out in September 2014.
During the 12 years of war in Yemen, control over al-Hazm has shifted several times, with the Houthis seizing the city in March 2020.
The governorate remains highly coveted due to its expansive border with Saudi Arabia and its direct geographic links to five pivotal governorates: Hadramout, Saada, Sanaa, Amran and oil-rich Marib and close to the capital, Sanaa.
Al-Jawf also acts as a vital defensive shield for Marib, controlled by government forces, preventing the Houthis from advancing into the eastern regions. It is also a gateway to major Houthi strongholds in northern Yemen.
Field Commander Colonel Rabie Al-Qurashi said government forces have been able to win complete control over the strategic Huwaishan mountain range, east of al-Hazm city. He said it is the first line of defence for the Houthis in the eastern axis and control over the rugged region would give government forces the ability to disrupt rebel supply routes.
“Government forces succeeded in breaking that defensive format with partial control over the Al-Alam front road,” Al-Qurashi said. “The government advance represents a beginning to tighten the noose on the Houthis in the upper al-Labanat camp,” which is regarded as a vital eastern gateway to Sanaa.
Ali Al-Dahab, a military and strategic affairs researcher, said there are immense tactical benefits from holding this elevated terrain.
“The recent advances of government forces in Al-Jawf are a military transformation that serves the course of future operations for their arrival to al-Hazm city,” Al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“The government forces’ recovery of a number of heights there provides a military and psychological morale advantage and confuses the Houthis’ decisions, in addition to granting government forces monitoring, movement, and observation of Houthi supply lines and securing their own lines.”
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili said on X that recent military operations against Houthi positions in al-Jawf were “inflicting losses on the militia’s capabilities”.
The government dominates the vast eastern desert district of Khabb wa ash Sha’af, representing 82 percent of the governorate’s total area. The Houthis control the provincial capital, al-Hazm, and 10 other districts.
Security and political affairs researcher Brigadier General Ahmed Al-Awadhi stressed the importance of “continuous but not rapid” government advances in the area.
“The advances of government forces in Al-Jawf cannot be ignored or their importance underestimated,” Al-Awadhi told Al Jazeera.
“Control over heights or mountain ranges in the desert Al-Jawf governorate represents points of military strength regardless of their proximity to or distance from the governorate capital.”
The government forces advances in al-Jawf highlight a historical vulnerability for the Houthis, having suffered repeated defeats in battles in desert and open areas, he added.
The developments coincide with the Presidential Council’s appointment of Major General Amin Ali Al-Akimi as governor and military commander of al-Jawf.
“[His] reappointment… comes within the context of restructuring the theatre of operations and unifying the front,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst told Al Jazeera.
“Hailing from Dhu Hussein, a branch of the Daham Bakil tribe, Al-Akimi possesses tribal and military influence that could help mobilise tribes, overcome divisions and bolster momentum on the ground. However, translating this influence into sustainable gains remains contingent upon unifying command and control, coordinating operations across all battlefronts, securing military and logistical support and strengthening anti-corruption efforts to improve the efficient management of military resources.”
The Houthis say they have thwarted advances by government forces in al-Jawf and Marib.
Fighting has continued in other parts of Yemen as Houthi-affiliated media reported air strikes on an oil company facility in the Bajil district of Hodeidah, which coincide with fierce fighting further south.
Government forces repelled Houthi attacks in al-Aqroudh and on the Tur al-Baha front in Lahij governorate. Intense fighting continues in Taiz governorate.
The siege of Taiz City continues to strain medical infrastructure, with deliveries of food and fuel severely restricted. Civilians remain at risk from sniper fire from surrounding hillsides, authorities have warned.
Governor Nabil Shamsan said that hospitals are working at only 20 percent capacity, with 120 health centres entirely shut due to the siege.
“We urge the international community to secure at least one safe route between Taiz and Aden to enable citizen movement and the smooth entry of services, essential materials and goods,” Shamsan appealed to Al Jazeera.
More than 300,000 people have fled their homes in western Yemen due to the escalating fighting, leaving civilians highly vulnerable.

articles.title_orig: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.title_zh: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston detail their record-breaking merger and how their ‘shared vision’ will create a category leader in AI connectivity on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
Marvell Technology chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said the chipmaker’s historic $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum is a "once in a generation’ opportunity to unite two of the most dominating companies in the AI boom and create a "category leader."
Appearing alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston on "The Claman Countdown," Murphy detailed the companies’ record-breaking merger on Monday, predicting that the transaction will cement Marvell’s position at the forefront of AI connectivity.
"It's very rare that you can find two companies of the caliber of Lumentum and Marvell that are number one in their respective areas that find a moment in time where you can combine and create a category leader in a new category," he told anchor Liz Claman.
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD
The race to build AI infrastructure is accelerating as concerns grow over centralized technological power. (Noah Berger / Getty Images)
"This AI connectivity is going to be as consequential as… the compute category, or the memory category, the fab category, and the IP licensing category."
Murphy's comments follow the announcement of Marvell’s agreement to acquire Lumentum in a landmark $115 billion transaction, marking the largest merger between two publicly traded companies. The deal will unite two massive AI enablers, equipped with electrical and optical expertise, to address connectivity requirements for next-generation AI infrastructure .
MASSIVE AI BOOM PUTS ONE OF AMERICA’S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS ON PATH TO DOUBLE IN SIZE, CEO SAYS
"Both companies.are executing phenomenally well. And what we see, Liz, is a multiplying effect, where we're gonna do much better together in two years than we would on a standalone basis," Hurlston predicted.
Under the terms of the all-stock agreement, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each share held, according to Marvell’s announcement.
"It’s really a historic day for the two companies," Murphy said. "We're putting together basically the best-in-class leader in AI connectivity technology for semiconductors with the leader in photonics. And it is something that hasn't been done before."
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy (Right) appeared alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston (Left) on "The Claman Countdown" on Monday. (Left (Takaaki Iwabu/Bloomberg via Getty Images), Right (Lam Yik Fei/Bloomberg via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
Marvell designs artificial intelligence chips and technology that powers data centers , while Lumentum designs lasers and other optical components that use light to transmit data between chips and servers.
Murphy said Lumentum and Marvell, both headquartered in Northern California, have a "shared vision" and detailed how he believes the two tech companies will work better together than apart.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
"Together, because of the additional opportunity we see with each other, there's an opportunity to really outperform as a combined company," the Marvell CEO said.
Murphy, who said the merger has received "tremendous support" from hyperscalers, told FOX Business that he expects "significant" revenue synergies and other benefits once the companies are joined together.
AI chip giant Nvidia is a strategic investor in both Lumentum, which has a market value of around $76 billion, and Marvell, with a value of roughly $172 billion.
The Marvell-Lumentum deal has garnered "super positive" feedback from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Hurlston said. (Getty )
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Hurlston told FOX Business that Murphy discussed the potential Lumentum acquisition with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang early in the process, adding that reaction from Nvidia has been "super positive."
"Nvidia is invested in Marvell, Nvidia is invested in Lumentum. We think we can actually bring a lot more product to bear to Nvidia a lot more quickly in this combination," Hurlston said.

Apple is seeding the iOS 27.2 update for supported iPhone models with several new features and fixes for over 160 security vulnerabilities . The iOS update brings new languages to Siri AI, Apple Pencil (USB-C) support on the iPhone Duo , and a lot more.
Siri AI is now available in French, Korean, Japanese, Spanish, and Portuguese on the iPhone 15 Pro series and iPhone 16 models.
The iOS 27.2 update also introduces Suggestions in Messages, Shared Albums in Photos, and support for SynthID watermarks in Photos and Image Playground.
In the Apple TV app, users get a new Simple Profiles feature, along with improved Multiview, which now allows up to four live sports streams to play simultaneously.
Apple has also expanded FaceTime's Dual Capture feature to support group calls. The update also includes a redesigned Apple Music app with a new black-and-white icon.
Additionally, iOS 27.2 brings new controls to the Home app, adding further functionality to Apple's smart home platform.

articles.title_orig: China Lays Out Four Missions Leading to a Crewed Moon Landing
articles.title_zh: China Lays Out Four Missions Leading to a Crewed Moon Landing
articles.content_orig:
China has published a mission-by-mission schedule for landing astronauts on the Moon before 2030, about a year behind NASA's 2028 target, Ars Technica reported. It is the most detailed public account so far of the country's lunar program.
Wang Xiang presented the plan on October 31 at the 7th Manned Space Academic Conference. He is deputy chief designer of China's Manned Space Program and chief designer of its lunar exploration project.
The two-day event at Beihang University was hosted by the China Manned Space Agency. It drew more than 800 experts and scholars, BigGo Finance reported.
Slides from the presentation list these steps, according to Ars Technica:
BigGo Finance summarised the 2028 to 2030 window differently. It said Wenchang, the launch site in Hainan, will host three uncrewed lunar orbit verification missions and one crewed landing.
Three astronauts would make the trip, with two going down to the surface, Shattered reported, citing Chinese state media. The third would stay in orbit aboard Mengzhou.
China lacks a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V. So the crew ship and lander launch separately. Shattered said this lets controllers confirm the lander reached lunar orbit before the crew commits to the trip.
After docking in lunar orbit, the two astronauts move into the lander and descend. They lift off, dock with Mengzhou a second time and return to Earth in the spacecraft, BigGo Finance said.
Development is under way on the lander, a moonwalk spacesuit and a crewed lunar rover.
There is no Apollo 8 or Artemis II equivalent in this plan. In those missions, a crew flies to the Moon and returns without landing, Ars Technica noted. Mengzhou will still carry astronauts to the Tiangong space station in low-Earth orbit.
In August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency tested a high-fidelity mock-up of the 26-ton Lanyue lander near Beijing. Tethers simulated lunar gravity. On February 11, Mengzhou passed a maximum dynamic pressure abort test and splashed down safely at sea.
BigGo Finance described it as China's first at-sea recovery of a crewed spacecraft.
Mengzhou has also arrived at Wenchang for the 2027 test flight. On October 22, the agency asked Chinese institutions to propose payloads for the uncrewed Lanyue flight. Shattered reported a March 1, 2027 deadline for those proposals.
It also said no firm date has been given for the crewed mission.
Ars Technica said NASA's schedule depends on lunar landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin. A US landing could slip to 2030 or later. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has cancelled the Lunar Gateway space station.
He has also cancelled planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket.
Shattered reported that Artemis III is now a crewed Earth-orbit test in 2027. The first landing moves to Artemis IV, targeted for early 2028.

articles.title_zh: Web host Squarespace lays off 19% of its employees
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
Squarespace, the web company that helps customers build and host their own websites, is laying off about one-fifth of its workforce, in a move that will affect hundreds of jobs.
Jeff Seedman, a public relations specialist representing Squarespace, confirmed the layoffs to TechCrunch. The Verge initially reported the layoffs.
“Squarespace is restructuring its organization and reducing its global workforce by approximately 19%, representing around 300 employees,” said Seedman. “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth.”
Website building has changed immensely over the last few years as a result of the generative AI boom. “Vibe-coding” website builders, which only require simple prompts from users to spin up functional front-end designs, have largely upended the industry, making it possible for users to create sites with significantly less effort.
These kinds of sites have become an increasingly central part of the website-building business. Last year, web host rival Wix bought Base44 for $80 million . Similar offerings, like Lovable, have generated significant investor interest; Lovable raised a $400 million Series C round in August that valued the company at $13.3 billion. Google also recently launched Stitch , a feature that allows users to swiftly generate user-interface designs.
Squarespace has also begun a big push into AI. In 2024, the company launched an AI tool called Blueprint. The company also recently announced Forma, an upcoming AI native platform, whose waitlist users can join .
Squarespace was founded in 2004 and went public in 2021 at a $10 billion valuation. However, the company struggled in the ensuing years to generate enthusiastic public market interest. Squarespace ultimately decided to go private again by way of a $7 billion private equity deal in 2024.
An earlier version of this report incorrectly stated that Squarespace had not yet launched AI tools; the story has been updated.

articles.title_zh: As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
articles.content_orig:
The conflict pits Morocco, which considers the region its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks a separate state
At 51, Binina Mohamed is as old as the conflict that drove her from the Western Sahara region into a refugee camp in southern Algeria, where she has spent her life among tens of thousands of others facing a similar fate.
The confrontation over her native land, often described as Africa’s longest-running territorial dispute, was brought back into focus this weekend by a UN Security ‌Council row that led to the end of a decades-old peacekeeping mission there.
The Western Sahara conflict pits Morocco, which considers the territory its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, a political and military organisation that has been seeking a separate state there since the departure of former colonial power Spain in 1976. Peacekeepers have watched over the territory since 1991, when the UN brokered a ceasefire ending years of guerrilla warfare between the two sides.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
articles.title_zh: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
articles.content_orig:
A new rule stops the model from rebuilding specific existing games, but developers say it also blocks their own projects.
Anthropic's Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model have reportedly begun to refuse some tasks related to copying video games and reverse engineering, according to a recent report .
The refusals may be linked to a new rule that tells the model not to recreate a specific existing game. An X/Twitter user known as Chasm shared the alleged rule's text, which reads, "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." Developers are also complaining on GitHub that Claude Code stops game-related work, including projects they say are their own. Some users say it also refuses generic tasks, such as analyzing a crash dump or using the Reverse Engineer Anything tool.
Anthropic has not made a standalone announcement, but Tbreak reports that the company confirmed the change through a statement by one of its staff members. Two sentences were added to the Claude Code prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating other people's games, and the company says it will keep adjusting the balance. Original games, genre games, and projects made from the user's own designs and assets should still work.
The change comes as more AI-made game clones appear on Steam; for example, Steam Next Fest was reportedly flooded with them.

articles.title_orig: New CB90 CX Is Bigger, Optionally Crewed Evolution Of Saab’s Proven Combat Boat
articles.title_zh: New CB90 CX Is Bigger, Optionally Crewed Evolution Of Saab’s Proven Combat Boat
articles.content_orig:
Home » Saab unveils optionally crewed CB90 CX ahead of Euronaval 2026
Saab has unveiled a larger, optionally crewed variant of its Combat Boat 90 (CB90) fast assault craft designed to expand the role of the combat boat beyond troop transport to a multimission combat platform.
The new variant, known as CB90 Capability X (CB90 CX), will initially be offered in three configurations: intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), anti-ship warfare, and short-range air-defence (SHORAD).
Sweden is the launch customer, and the first boat is undergoing final acceptance trials ahead of delivery.
Briefing media online on 30 October, Anders Hellman, head of Saab’s business unit Docksta, said CB90 CX was the company’s response to a rapidly changing maritime security environment, where naval forces need to detect threats earlier, distribute capability across more platforms, and operate with greater flexibility.
He pointed to incidents involving critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea, the use of small distributed systems against conventional naval forces in the Black Sea, and attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea.
“These are of course different environments, but I think the lesson is similar,” he said. “Naval forces need to see more, they have to move faster, and most importantly, they need to distribute their capabilities across more platforms. So, the idea is quite simple: we have taken a proven combat boat and turned it into a distributed capability.”
With an overall length of 18 m, a beam of 4 m, and a draught of 1.1 m, CB90 CX is 1.4 m longer and 0.3 m wider than the CB90 Next Generation (NG) variant. Powered by two 1,100 hp engines driving waterjets, the boat has a top speed of more than 40 kt fully loaded and a range of more than 300 n miles at around 40 kt. It can carry a crew complement of up to 10 personnel.
According to Hellman, the larger hull has increased payload capacity by more than 50% compared with CB90 NG, on a like-for-like basis, from around 3 tonnes to “well beyond” 5 tonnes. It has also significantly improved seakeeping, he said. The boat is built to the DNV HSLC R2 class notation, which enables it to operate up to 100 n miles from a safe haven in summer and 50 n miles in winter. “From a Baltic perspective, this gives us free manoeuvrability within the entire Baltic,” he said.
Asked by Naval News whether the larger hull had required any trade-offs, Hellman said the company had been able “to keep the same user experience and feel” of the baseline vessel, which is centred around simplicity of design, and ease of use and operation. He added that the profile of the vessel has been kept low, both to limit its signature and to ensure it remains transportable by road and air.
More significant than the hull changes, according to Hellman, is the vessel’s new common system architecture, known as Combat Core. This integrates ship automation, platform monitoring, fire control, and a new steer-by-wire system into a single digital backbone, enabling capabilities to be added and upgraded throughout the boat’s lifecycle. The Combat Core is based on an open architecture, allowing customers to integrate their own sensors and weapons.
Saab’s Autonomous Ocean Core software is integrated with the Combat Core to provide the basis for uncrewed operations. According to Hellman, all CB90 CX boats are prepared for uncrewed operations from the outset, enabling the boat to be controlled from a remote station or through AI functionality. “This doesn’t take people out of the decision-making process, but it gives the operators much better flexibility in how they use people and platforms,” he noted.
Saab is initially producing the CB90 CX in three customer-driven configurations, although Hellman stressed these are only a starting point.
The ISR configuration is equipped with a Saab Sea Giraffe 1X X-band 3D surveillance radar, which rotates at 60 rpm to provide 360-degree coverage of air and surface targets and has an air detection range of more than 100 km. The radar sits on a newly designed mast that extends to 11 m, enabling the boat to see over islands in the archipelago. In its lowest 4 m position the mast allows unrestricted operations at speed. A Saab Trackfire remote weapon station armed with a 12.7 mm or 30 mm gun provides counter-uncrewed aerial system protection.
The anti-ship version was shown during the briefing armed with MBDA’s Marte ER sea-skimming fire-and-forget missile, which has a range or more than 100 km with external targeting data. Amphibious forces have traditionally carried missile teams ashore to set up and engage naval targets. With the missile system onboard, “the combat boat can do more than transport the capability. It becomes part of the strike capability itself,” Hellman said, adding that it also enables forces to regroup much faster and with greater manoeuvrability. He noted that Sweden’s amphibious battalion is acquiring a different missile, and that the Marte ER fit is intended to demonstrate the platform’s flexibility.
The SHORAD variant is armed with Rheinmetall’s Seasnake 30 naval gun, which fires KCE-30 30 x 173 mm ammunition. Its primary targets are helicopters, drones, and loitering munitions, with ground targets, small landing craft, and small patrol boats as secondary targets. In February 2026 FMV, Sweden’s defence procurement agency, ordered an initial eight Seasnake 30 systems to arm its CB90s under the Amphibious Battalion 2030 modernisation programme. “The big change is that short-range air defence becomes mobile; it can move and appear when it is needed,” Hellman said.
He said the three configurations are intended to work together, operating in different locations but connected as one force, taking the combat boat “from carrying the fighting force to becoming part of it”.
Saab is also developing additional capabilities for CB90 CX, including the option to launch drones – with both tube-launched systems and quadcopters under consideration – and torpedoes. Hellman said the company has a parallel development track for further configurations.
Sweden has a total of 36 CB90s on order, including 10 ordered in June 2024, 22 in 2025, and a further four added in the first half of 2026.
The CB90 CX will be offered alongside the CB90 NG, which Saab will keep in production. To meet anticipated demand, the company is building a new site at Docksta that will double its production capacity. Hellman said its focus markets are NATO and allied nations, particularly in the Baltic and Mediterranean regions. More than 300 CB90s are in service with nine navies.

articles.title_orig: China Tech Stocks Get Fresh Lifeline From Beijing
articles.title_zh: China Tech Stocks Get Fresh Lifeline From Beijing
articles.content_orig:
Alibaba BABA , JD.com JD and PDD Holdings PDD moved higher in U.S. premarket trading Monday after Chinese regulators signaled a fresh effort to stabilize the country's battered stock market.
The move follows an 8.5% October drop in the CSI 300 , its worst monthly performance since early 2016. The benchmark had also fallen for 12 consecutive weeks, according to TipRanks.
Beijing is now stepping in with more liquidity.
The People's Bank of China said it will conduct a new swap operation Tuesday that could inject more than 100 billion yuan, or roughly $15 billion , into the equity market. Thirty-one brokerages and fund companies have already applied for quotas worth more than 100 billion yuan.
The swap facility allows securities firms, insurers and fund managers to exchange eligible assets for more liquid central-bank assets, giving them additional capacity to buy stocks.
China is also making its relending program for share repurchases and stake increases a long-term mechanism , while cutting the program's interest rate to 1% from 1.25% .
Regulators are applying pressure directly as well.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission urged major index constituents and leading technology companies to actively buy back shares , while also encouraging newer ETFs and fund managers to increase equity exposure during the downturn. Officials are separately studying whether to ease margin rules to improve market liquidity.
The policy response helped lift sentiment Monday, with the Shanghai Composite gaining 1.1% and the CSI 300 also moving higher.
Alibaba, JD and PDD have been caught in the broader decline as investors grapple with weak Chinese consumption, persistent property-sector problems and pressure across technology shares.
I think the key point here is that Beijing is sending a clearer message that it does not want the equity selloff to spiral.
For Alibaba, JD and PDD, that matters because their stocks have increasingly been trading on macro sentiment and policy risk, not just company fundamentals.
The latest measures can improve liquidity and potentially put a floor under sentiment.
But they do not fix the underlying issues by themselves.
China still needs stronger consumption, better economic momentum and more confidence in corporate earnings for the rally to become durable.
For investors, the key things to watch are how much of the new liquidity is actually deployed, whether corporate buybacks accelerate, and whether China follows these market-support steps with broader fiscal or economic stimulus .
The immediate signal is supportive.
The harder question is whether Beijing can turn that support into a lasting recovery.

articles.title_orig: How China Might Target US Midterms - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.title_zh: How China Might Target US Midterms - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.content_orig:
No research shows Chinese propaganda or disinformation playing a pivotal role in the midterm elections, particularly when compared to Russia’s aggressive attempts. Yet significant blind spots exist. If it desired, Beijing is well-positioned to shape political debate through the WeChat app and through Chinese AI models.
Rather than shifting control of Congress, Beijing’s goal would likely be to reduce the presence of known Communist Party critics, particularly those serving in the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. Created by Congress in October 2000, the Commission monitors Chinese human rights and rule of law.
Several competitive races feature Commission members, including former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio and current Commission Chair Dan Sullivan in Alaska. House races in Iowa and Virginia involve current Commission members Zach Nunn and Jen Kiggans. Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate in Iowa, is on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, another Congressional body critical of the regime.
Texas looks particularly sensitive for a different reason. WeChat , a messaging and multi-function app, has an estimated 1.5 million US users, concentrated in states with large Chinese American populations. Chinese Americans make up roughly one percent of Texas’s population .
Chinese state-sponsored censorship on WeChat is well-documented. A 2025 University of Texas study based on interviews with 20 Chinese Americans in Texas detailed how political misinformation circulates on the platform. One young interviewee described how her father read that an Asian American woman had been elected mayor of Boston months before the actual election.
“He just accepts everything he reads, and then he just forwards it,” she said. “My mother-in-law, too.”
Cultural and social pressures reduce willingness to correct misinformation in family or friend groups. “It doesn’t feel right for me to talk bad to my elders, especially in the group chat setting,” a 19-year-old Chinese American explained.
In this environment, the app is powerful. “A lot of people don’t know who to vote for, so they are easily swayed,” another interviewee commented. “It is a big political platform, and a lot of people will just blindly follow.”
The 2026 elections are the first to take place in an environment where AI chatbots are widely available. About one-fifth of Americans plan to use AI tools to help learn about candidates or inform voting decisions, according to a recent survey . Most will turn to American models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Perplexity, but many US developers are increasingly relying on Chinese-origin models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, allowing them to enter the US information environment.
These models reflect the Chinese government’s official stances on domestic politics and human rights. Censorship and propaganda have also been found in responses to questions about US press freedom and elections.
One study examined Chinese AI models’ responses to questions about the upcoming US elections. Conducted by a research group based in Europe, researchers tested seven AI models (five US and two Chinese) with a set of 20 polling-style questions.
All models proved relatively consistent and offered mixed results in terms of partisan preferences. The two Chinese models did not diverge sharply from their US counterparts in their responses. DeepSeek, for example, selected the Democratic option on two questions about which party’s candidate it would select for Congress and which party it prefers to control Congress. So did Claude and Perplexity (99% on one of the questions). By contrast, Qwen chose Democrats 55% and 75% of the time, respectively.
The results are striking for what they show about the leeway allowed the Chinese models to comment on US versus Chinese politics. DeepSeek offered critical assessments of the US president’s job performance. Asking the same questions about Chinese President Xi Jinping would almost certainly produce refusals or strictly glowing reviews.
Major holes remain in our understanding of where and how Chinese Communist Party-linked electoral influence could be occurring. Researchers, election monitors, and others focused on election integrity should address these gaps — particularly before the 2028 elections.
Sarah Cook is founder of China Rights Analytics and Advising LLC and author of the UnderReported China newsletter.

articles.title_orig: 'Exceptionally horrific strike' — Russian bombs hit school used as humanitarian aid center in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, killing 26
articles.title_zh: 'Exceptionally horrific strike' — Russian bombs hit school used as humanitarian aid center in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, killing 26
articles.content_orig:
Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast crater
At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubble
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
The Russian strikes left a huge crater where Ukrainian officials say people were sheltering
Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".
He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in the next few days after negotiations were suspended in February, with Moscow stepping up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
However, no major breakthrough is expected at the talks that are likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices slide as hopes rise for potential US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Oil prices slide as hopes rise for potential US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude , the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel.
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.
Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.
